questions.s: Which quality means telling the truth and not deceiving others?
o: Honesty
Ambition
Curiosity
Loyalty
questions.e: Honesty is being truthful in word and deed. Loyalty is faithfulness to a person or group, and it can exist without truthfulness.

questions.s: Which quality means refusing to compromise one's moral principles even when no one is watching?
o: Popularity
Flexibility
Obedience
Integrity
questions.e: Integrity is wholeness of character: acting on one's principles consistently. Obedience means following orders, which may or may not be right.

questions.s: Treating every person according to the same fair rules, without favouring friends or relatives, is called
o: impartiality
generosity
sympathy
diplomacy
questions.e: Impartiality means judging fairly without bias. Generosity is giving freely and does not by itself ensure fairness.

questions.s: A judge decides a case on the evidence alone and ignores the fact that one side is his relative. This shows
o: empathy
obedience
ambition
impartiality
questions.e: Setting aside personal ties to judge on evidence is impartiality. Empathy involves sharing feelings and would not by itself ensure a fair verdict.

questions.s: A manager openly publishes how funds were spent so that anyone can check. This practice is called
o: secrecy
competition
transparency
delegation
questions.e: Transparency means open information that allows others to check conduct. Delegation is handing work to others.

questions.s: Giving a job to a relative who is less qualified than other candidates is called
o: meritocracy
diplomacy
mentorship
nepotism
questions.e: Nepotism is favouring relatives in appointments. Meritocracy is the opposite: choosing by ability.

questions.s: Selecting people for jobs and promotions strictly on ability and performance is called
o: nepotism
meritocracy
bribery
seniority
questions.e: Meritocracy rewards demonstrated merit. Seniority rewards length of service, which may differ from merit.

questions.s: Offering money to an official to obtain an unfair advantage is
o: charity
negotiation
bribery
trade
questions.e: Bribery corrupts fair decisions. Charity is given for the welfare of others, with no gain demanded.

questions.s: A person has a personal interest that could influence his official duty. This situation is known as
o: a code of conduct
an audit trail
a quorum
a conflict of interest
questions.e: A conflict of interest arises when private gain could affect public duty. The correct response is usually to disclose it and step aside from the decision.

questions.s: An engineer is asked to choose a contractor and learns that his brother's firm has bid. The most ethical step is to
o: choose his brother because he trusts him
quietly reject his brother's bid to look fair
say nothing and treat all bids alike
declare the connection and let others decide
questions.e: Disclosing the link and stepping aside protects fairness. Secretly rejecting or favouring the brother is itself bias, and silence hides a conflict of interest.

questions.s: Presenting another person's work as your own is called
o: paraphrasing
research
citation
plagiarism
questions.e: Plagiarism is dishonest use of someone else's words or ideas without credit. Citation is the honest alternative of acknowledging a source.

questions.s: An employee reports serious fraud in his company to the proper authority, at some risk to himself. This is called
o: whistleblowing
eavesdropping
gossiping
bargaining
questions.e: Whistleblowing is exposing wrongdoing in the public interest. Gossiping is idle talk about people and serves no such purpose.

questions.s: Which of these is the best example of moral courage?
o: Following the crowd in order to avoid any trouble with other people
Speaking up against an injustice when it is unpopular
Keeping quiet about a wrong in order to protect one's own job
Boasting about one's achievements before a large audience
questions.e: Moral courage is doing right despite personal risk. The other choices avoid the risk or are about pride.

questions.s: Understanding and sharing the feelings of another person is called
o: rivalry
pride
empathy
suspicion
questions.e: Empathy helps us see a situation from another person's view. Suspicion is distrust of others.

questions.s: What is the difference between empathy and sympathy?
o: Empathy is a form of anger; sympathy is a form of joy
Empathy feels with another person; sympathy feels for them
Empathy and sympathy have exactly the same meaning
Empathy is a form of fear; sympathy is a form of hope
questions.e: Empathy means sharing another's perspective or feelings, while sympathy is concern or pity from outside. The other pairs are unrelated emotions.

questions.s: Concern for the welfare of others without expecting any reward is called
o: egoism
rivalry
altruism
thrift
questions.e: Altruism puts others' interests first. Egoism puts one's own interest first.

questions.s: Which of these is a quality shown by a person who is humble?
o: He boasts about his successes in front of colleagues
He avoids learning anything from other people
He accepts correction and credits others
He blames others whenever he makes an error
questions.e: Humility is an accurate and modest view of oneself, which lets a person learn. The other behaviours show pride.

questions.s: Showing thanks for what one has received is called
o: envy
gratitude
greed
pride
questions.e: Gratitude is acknowledging kindness and blessings. Envy is resentment of what others have.

questions.s: Which of these best describes forgiveness?
o: Pretending that the wrong never happened at all
Choosing to let go of resentment towards a wrongdoer
Taking revenge in exactly equal measure to the harm
Telling everyone in the area about what was done
questions.e: Forgiveness is a deliberate release of resentment. It does not mean denying that the wrong happened, though justice may still be sought.

questions.s: The principle that an accused person is innocent until proved guilty is called
o: the presumption of innocence
the burden of conscience that every judge must carry
moral relativism as applied to criminal cases
the common courtesy that a court extends to all
questions.e: The presumption of innocence is a basic part of fair trial. It places the burden of proof on the accuser.

questions.s: Equality means treating everyone the same; equity means
o: giving everyone identical amounts regardless of their different needs
giving each person what they need for a fair outcome
favouring the strongest members of any group
ignoring individual differences between people entirely
questions.e: Equity adjusts support to need, for example more help for students who start with fewer resources. Identical treatment may leave unfair gaps.

questions.s: Which statement best distinguishes 'legal' from 'ethical'?
o: Whatever is legal is always ethical as well
An act can be legal yet still unethical
Whatever is ethical is always legal as well
The two words mean exactly the same thing in law
questions.e: Law sets minimum rules, while ethics asks what is right. Some legal acts, such as deliberately humiliating a colleague, are still wrong. Some laws can also be unjust.

questions.s: Distributive justice is concerned with
o: the punishment of those who have broken the law of the land
the speed with which a court decides every single case
the careful writing and signing of every contract
the fair sharing of benefits and burdens in society
questions.e: Distributive justice asks who should get what. Retributive justice concerns punishment, and procedural justice the fairness of the process.

questions.s: Retributive justice is mainly concerned with
o: giving offenders the punishment they deserve
sharing wealth fairly among all of the citizens
forgiving every offence that anyone commits
lowering the taxes that people have to pay
questions.e: Retributive justice links punishment to the wrongdoing. Sharing wealth is a question of distributive justice.

questions.s: The moral theory that says the right action is the one that produces the greatest good for the greatest number is
o: deontology
relativism
egoism
utilitarianism
questions.e: Utilitarianism, associated with Bentham and Mill, judges actions by their consequences. Deontology judges by duty and rules.

questions.s: The moral theory in which an action is right if it follows duty or rules, whatever the outcome, is
o: utilitarianism
egoism
deontology
relativism
questions.e: Deontology, strongly associated with Kant, stresses duties. Utilitarianism looks at results.

questions.s: Which philosopher is most closely linked with the 'categorical imperative'?
o: John Stuart Mill
Immanuel Kant
Aristotle
Thomas Hobbes
questions.e: Kant argued one should act only on principles that could become universal laws. Mill was a utilitarian and Aristotle a virtue ethicist.

questions.s: Aristotle's 'golden mean' suggests that a virtue lies
o: always at the most extreme point of behaviour
in the complete avoidance of all emotion
in simply obeying whatever the majority does
between the extremes of excess and deficiency
questions.e: Courage, for example, lies between recklessness and cowardice. The mean is not a mathematical average but fitting behaviour for the situation.

questions.s: The view that right and wrong depend entirely on the culture or individual is known as
o: moral absolutism
utilitarianism
moral relativism
stoicism
questions.e: Moral relativism denies universal moral standards. Absolutism holds that some acts are right or wrong everywhere.

questions.s: The idea of choosing rules of society without knowing one's own place in it, proposed by John Rawls, is called the
o: golden rule
veil of ignorance
social contract
state of nature
questions.e: Behind the veil of ignorance, people choose fair rules because they might end up in any position. The social contract is a different idea about why people consent to government.

questions.s: The saying 'Treat others as you would like to be treated' is known as the
o: Iron Law
Silver Mean
Golden Rule
Final Cause
questions.e: A form of the Golden Rule appears in many religious and philosophical traditions. The other names do not refer to a moral principle.

questions.s: Which of the Ten Commandments of Judaism and Christianity forbids taking what belongs to another?
o: You shall not steal
You shall not kill
You shall not bear false witness
Honour your father and mother
questions.e: The prohibition of theft is the commandment against taking what belongs to another. The other commandments listed are about life, truthfulness and respect for parents.

questions.s: Ahimsa, a central principle of Jainism that is also important in Hinduism and Buddhism, means
o: charity
sacrifice
non-violence
silence
questions.e: Ahimsa means not harming living beings. Jain teaching applies it strictly, including to thoughts and diet.

questions.s: In Hinduism, 'dharma' refers to
o: a special form of daily prayer
righteous duty and moral order
a major festival of lights
the name of a holy river
questions.e: Dharma means duty and right conduct appropriate to one's role. The festival of lights is Diwali.

questions.s: The Noble Eightfold Path in Buddhism includes
o: fasting for forty days at a time every year
a pilgrimage to the city of Jerusalem by every follower
giving a tenth of one's income to the temple each year
right speech, right action and right livelihood
questions.e: Right speech, right action and right livelihood are three of its eight parts. Fasting and tithing belong to other traditions or are not part of the path.

questions.s: The founder of Buddhism was
o: Guru Nanak
Zoroaster
Siddhartha Gautama
Confucius
questions.e: Siddhartha Gautama became known as the Buddha, the awakened one. Guru Nanak founded Sikhism and Zoroaster is linked with Zoroastrianism.

questions.s: Which of these is one of the five moral precepts followed by lay Buddhists?
o: Refraining from taking life
Fasting on one day of every week
Giving up all possessions on entering a temple
Praying at dawn facing a particular direction
questions.e: The first precept is to abstain from killing. The others are not among the five precepts.

questions.s: Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism, was born in a town now known as
o: Nankana Sahib
Kartarpur
Amritsar
Lahore
questions.e: Nankana Sahib in Punjab, Pakistan, is his birthplace. Kartarpur is where he spent his last years.

questions.s: The Sikh practice of 'langar' is
o: a free community meal open to everyone
a special form of fasting before a festival
a pilgrimage to a holy place each year
a tax paid by traders in a market
questions.e: Langar is a communal kitchen where people of every religion and background sit together and eat. It expresses equality and service.

questions.s: The Sikh teaching of 'vand chakna' encourages followers to
o: fast daily
live as hermits
avoid all trade
share with others
questions.e: The three principles of Sikh life are remembering God, earning honestly and sharing with others. Vand chakna means sharing.

questions.s: The Zoroastrian ethic is summed up in
o: truth, silence and patience in daily life
prayer, fasting and charity throughout the year
good thoughts, good words, good deeds
duty, harvest and rest in each season
questions.e: Humata, hukhta, hvarshta, meaning good thoughts, good words and good deeds, is the core moral motto. The other triads are not that motto.

questions.s: The Parable of the Good Samaritan in Christian teaching shows
o: help should be given only to one's own relatives
help should be given to a stranger in need
religious rituals matter more than acts of kindness
travel on the road is always very dangerous
questions.e: In the parable a traveller from a despised group helps an injured man whom others passed by. It teaches compassion beyond community.

questions.s: Which statement about charity in the world's religions is accurate?
o: Only one religion encourages helping those in need
No religion has ever mentioned helping those in need
Islam, Judaism, Christianity, Hinduism, Buddhism and Sikhism all encourage it
Helping the needy is forbidden in most major religions
questions.e: Concern for the poor is a shared moral value, expressed as zakat, tzedakah, dana, seva and similar practices. No tradition forbids it.

questions.s: Jain teaching of 'anekantavada' encourages
o: the holding of one single fixed opinion
silence during every debate or discussion
the rejection of every view that differs from one's own
respect for many points of view
questions.e: Anekantavada means many-sidedness: truth has several aspects, so one should listen to other views. It is often cited as a basis for tolerance.

questions.s: The Bhagavad Gita teaches that one should perform one's duty
o: only when it is done for a personal reward
only for those who are related to the person
only when it is done in public places
without attachment to the results
questions.e: It stresses selfless action. Doing duty for reward alone is the opposite emphasis.

questions.s: Confucius placed great stress on 'ren', which is best described as
o: military strength and discipline in an army
skill in trade and in the keeping of accounts
obedience to rulers whatever they command
humaneness and kindness towards others
questions.e: Ren is the virtue of goodwill and human feeling. The other options are different concerns.

questions.s: In his speech of 11 August 1947, Quaid-e-Azam said that citizens would be free to go to their temples, mosques or places of worship, and that a person's religion
o: has nothing to do with the business of the state
must be recorded on every public document
decides who may hold public office
must be that of the majority
questions.e: He told the Constituent Assembly that a person may belong to any religion, caste or creed and that this has nothing to do with the business of the state.

questions.s: Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights states that all human beings are born
o: rich or poor by destiny
with different value according to nation
free and equal in dignity and rights
with duties but no rights
questions.e: The UDHR, adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1948, begins with this statement of equal dignity. It does not rank people by birth or nation.

questions.s: Ayesha finds a purse with money and an identity card on a bus seat. What should she do?
o: Hand it to the driver or the police so the owner can be found
Keep the money and throw away the identity card at home
Leave it on the seat without telling anyone about it
Spend the money on treating her friends at a restaurant
questions.e: Returning lost property respects the owner's right to it. Keeping it, even if only the money, is theft by finding.

questions.s: Which action shows respect for public property?
o: Writing slogans on the wall of a bus shelter
Breaking street lights for fun after dark
Using a park bench without damaging it
Taking pipes from a public water tap for use at home
questions.e: Public property belongs to everyone, so using it with care respects others' shared right. Damaging it harms the whole community.

questions.s: A driver stops at a red light at midnight on an empty road, believing that rules matter even when no one is watching. This shows
o: fear of the traffic warden
integrity
a habit with no moral value
a wish to waste time
questions.e: Keeping a rule when unobserved, because the rule matters, shows integrity. Fear of being caught would be a weaker motive and is not what the driver believes here.

questions.s: A student sees a classmate copying in an exam. Which response best protects fairness?
o: Join in so that everyone is equal
Ignore it because it is not her paper
Report it to the invigilator quietly
Announce it loudly to the whole class
questions.e: Honest results depend on fair exams, so telling the invigilator is the fair step. Publicly shaming the classmate is harsher than needed.

questions.s: A pharmacist notices that a customer has been given the wrong dose by mistake. The most professional response is to
o: correct it at once and inform the doctor
say nothing in order to avoid any embarrassment
correct it quietly and tell no one at all about it
let the customer decide what is to be done about it
questions.e: Patient safety comes first, and professional duty includes reporting the error. Hiding it risks harm and repeats the mistake.

questions.s: A teacher, Mr Rashid, has a relative in his class who deserves lower marks than the others. He should
o: mark by the same standard as for every other student
raise the marks slightly in order to please the family
lower the marks so that he can look strict to others
ask another student to do the marking in his place
questions.e: Fair marking means one standard for all. Raising or lowering marks because of a relationship is bias in either direction.

questions.s: A journalist receives a story that would damage a rival company, but cannot verify it. The ethical choice is to
o: publish at once to be first
publish it with a small disclaimer
leave out the company's name only
check the facts before publishing
questions.e: Responsible reporting depends on accuracy. Publishing unverified claims can ruin a reputation unjustly.

questions.s: An accountant is told by his employer to alter the figures to avoid tax. Which is the most ethical response?
o: Obey, since the employer carries all of the responsibility
Obey, but keep a private note of the instruction given
Alter only a small part of the figures to be on the safe side
Refuse and report the matter through proper channels
questions.e: Falsifying records is dishonest and illegal. A private note does not undo taking part in the wrong, and a small alteration is still a wrong.

questions.s: A manager takes credit for a plan that her junior, Sana, designed. What is wrong with this?
o: Nothing is wrong, since managers always lead the team
It saves time and effort for the whole company
It is dishonest and unfair to the person who did it
It follows the usual order of hierarchy in an office
questions.e: Giving credit to those who earned it is basic fairness. Hierarchy does not justify claiming another person's work.

questions.s: Hamza promised to help a friend move house on Saturday, but then gets an invitation to a party. What is the most ethical choice?
o: Cancel at the last moment without telling the friend
Send a quick message and stay on at the party
Keep the promise unless a serious reason arises
Go to the party and apologise to the friend later
questions.e: A promise creates a duty that should not be set aside for convenience. A pleasant invitation is not a serious reason.

questions.s: Which of these shows ethical leadership?
o: Blaming juniors for every error that occurs
Keeping rules for others but not for oneself
Taking responsibility when the team fails
Hiding mistakes from one's own superiors
questions.e: A good leader accepts accountability. Blaming others or hiding faults breaks the trust of the team.

questions.s: A shopkeeper sells a product knowing that it has a fault but does not tell the buyer. This is
o: dishonest, as it hides important information
acceptable if the price of the item is low enough
acceptable because the buyer may not notice the fault
honest, as the seller has not told any spoken lie
questions.e: Deceiving by hiding a known fault is dishonest even without a spoken lie. The buyer's decision depends on full information.

questions.s: During a flood, a trader raises the price of flour sharply because people are desperate. This is unethical because
o: prices of goods must never change at all
traders in every city are required to be poor
flour is not an important item in daily life
it exploits people's need for profit
questions.e: Taking advantage of a crisis puts profit above human welfare. Fair pricing in an emergency respects the dignity of customers.

questions.s: A doctor learns that a patient's illness is serious. Which approach is most ethical?
o: Hide it from the patient in order to avoid distress
Explain the condition honestly and with compassion
Tell only distant relatives and not the patient himself
Speak in vague terms that leave the patient confused
questions.e: Patients have the right to know about their own health, and honesty can be gentle. Withholding the truth removes their ability to decide.

questions.s: A company discharges waste into a river near a village to cut costs. Which principle does this violate most directly?
o: Responsibility for the harm done to others
The right of an owner to pay himself a bonus
The rule that seniority decides every matter
The freedom of competition between companies
questions.e: Polluting a shared resource harms the villagers' health. Cost-saving cannot justify damage to others.

questions.s: A student uses a friend's essay and submits it as her own. Her fault is
o: dishonesty and plagiarism
helpfulness
creativity
efficiency
questions.e: Presenting another's work as one's own is plagiarism, and it harms both honest students and the learning process.

questions.s: A person is sent a rumour about a neighbour through a messaging app. The most responsible action is to
o: forward it to everyone at once
stop and check before forwarding
add some details to make it clearer
post it publicly with a comment
questions.e: Spreading unverified claims can damage a person unfairly. Verifying, or not sharing at all, is responsible behaviour.

questions.s: Ali is asked to take a job for which he lacks the skills, in a field where lives depend on competence. He should
o: accept and learn the work as he goes along
accept the post to please his relative
be honest about his limits and decline
pretend to have the skills that are needed
questions.e: Professional ethics requires working only within one's competence, especially where safety is involved. Pretending would be dishonest and dangerous.

questions.s: An office worker, Noor, notices that a colleague regularly leaves early but signs as present. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Do the same, so that everyone is treated equally in the office
Ignore the matter for as long as it goes on
Tell all the staff at lunch what has been seen
Speak to the colleague, and if it continues, report it
questions.e: Raising the matter directly first, then reporting, deals with it fairly. Copying the behaviour or gossiping adds to the wrong.

questions.s: A principal receives an application from a poor but very able student and another from a wealthy student of lower marks who offers a donation. He should
o: admit by merit and not accept the donation as a condition
admit the wealthy donor's child in return for the money
decide the matter by tossing a coin in front of both parents
admit neither student, to avoid any kind of dispute
questions.e: Selecting on ability keeps admission fair. A donation in exchange for a place is a form of bribery.

questions.s: A pilot is tired after a long duty but has been asked to take one more flight. The ethical choice is to
o: accept to avoid disappointing the airline
fly but let the co-pilot decide
refuse if fatigue endangers safety
fly and hope for the best
questions.e: Safety of passengers is the overriding duty. Fatigue can impair judgement as much as other risks.

questions.s: The head of a charity uses donated funds for a personal holiday and plans to repay it later. This is
o: acceptable if repaid
acceptable if no one finds out
acceptable because the head works hard
a breach of trust even if repaid
questions.e: Donations are held in trust for a stated purpose, and using them privately betrays donors. Repayment does not remove the breach.

questions.s: Imran is a junior engineer. He discovers that a bridge design his firm approved has a flaw that could endanger lives, but his senior says to ignore it. The strongest ethical obligation is to
o: obey the senior in order to keep his own job safe
resign quietly without telling anyone about the flaw at all
wait and see whether an accident occurs before saying anything
raise the concern through proper channels until it is dealt with
questions.e: Public safety outweighs loyalty to a superior. Staying silent or leaving without warning leaves the danger in place.

questions.s: A hospital has one ventilator and two patients who need it. Which method is generally regarded as the fairest way to choose?
o: Give it to the richer patient, who can pay a higher fee
Give it to the patient who has the larger number of relatives
Use an impartial rule such as medical need, not wealth
Give it to whichever patient is better known to the doctor
questions.e: Fair allocation uses relevant criteria like medical need, applied impartially. Wealth, connections and acquaintance are morally irrelevant.

questions.s: A police officer sees his close friend break a traffic law. Applying the law equally means he should
o: let the friend go because of friendship
treat the friend as he would any citizen
fine the friend double to prove fairness
warn only strangers
questions.e: Equality before the law means no favour and no extra penalty. Doubling the fine is also unfair.

questions.s: Sara's friend asks her to lie to the teacher so that he can avoid punishment for a prank. The best response is to
o: refuse to lie but encourage her friend to admit it
lie to the teacher, since friendship must always come first
lie to the teacher, but only on this one occasion
blame some other student for the prank instead
questions.e: Honesty cannot be set aside to protect someone, and blaming another person adds a further wrong. Encouraging the friend to own up supports both honesty and loyalty.

questions.s: A cashier notices that her supervisor has charged a customer double. She should
o: say nothing, since it is not part of her own job
tell the other customers in the shop what has happened
wait until the customer himself complains about the bill
tell the supervisor and see that the customer is corrected
questions.e: Speaking up protects the customer and the business. Silence makes her part of an unfair practice.

questions.s: A person promises a loan to a friend but later finds he cannot afford it. The honest course is to
o: tell the friend as soon as possible
avoid meeting the friend for as long as he can
give a part of the loan and say nothing about the rest
pretend that he had forgotten all about the promise
questions.e: Telling the truth early lets the friend make other plans. Avoiding him or pretending forgetfulness adds deceit.

questions.s: A student leader, Faiz, receives money from the school to organise an event and has Rs 2,000 left over. The correct action is to
o: keep it as a small reward for his own efforts
spend it on his friends for a treat at the school
return the unused amount with a clear account
say that the amount was never given to him at all
questions.e: Funds given for a purpose must be accounted for. Unused money belongs to the institution.

questions.s: Which of the following is an ethical way to compete for a promotion?
o: Spread rumours about a rival to damage his name
Improve one's own skills and results
Hide a rival's files so that he misses a deadline
Offer a gift to the manager before the decision
questions.e: Fair competition relies on one's merit. Rumours, sabotage and gifts to the manager are unfair means.

questions.s: A restaurant owner finds that a cook has been using stale ingredients. The best response is to
o: ignore the matter in order to save the cost of food
remove the stale food and train the staff on hygiene
tell customers that all of the food is perfectly fine
fire the cook but keep using the same stale ingredients
questions.e: Customers' health is at stake, so the problem must be fixed at its source. Blaming one person does not remove the risk.

questions.s: A researcher finds that her results do not support her own theory. Which action best meets the standard of research ethics?
o: Change the data to fit her theory
Leave out the unwelcome results
Wait until another team publishes
Report the results honestly
questions.e: Scientific integrity means reporting what is found. Altering or omitting data is fabrication or selective reporting, which misleads others.

questions.s: A volunteer in a relief camp is asked by an official to give extra rations to his own relatives. The most ethical response is to
o: agree because he is an official
agree if the relatives are poor
give half to relatives and half to others
refuse and give by need
questions.e: Relief should be given according to need and not connections. Even poor relatives should get only what their need entitles them to, on the same basis as others.

questions.s: Tolerance in a society means
o: agreeing with every belief that other people may hold
accepting that others may hold different beliefs
avoiding all one's neighbours and their customs
forcing others to give up their own customs and habits
questions.e: Tolerance means respecting people's right to differ, without having to share their views. Forcing change is the opposite.

questions.s: Tolerance is NOT the same as
o: agreeing with everything others believe
respecting their right to hold different beliefs
living peacefully alongside them
listening to different views
questions.e: One can tolerate a view without accepting it. Tolerance is about respect for the person's rights, not agreement.

questions.s: Which is the best example of religious tolerance?
o: Allowing every community to worship freely
Mocking another group's festival in public
Banning all festivals from being held in public
Forcing everyone to use one common greeting and dress
questions.e: Respecting free worship is the heart of tolerance. Mockery and enforced uniformity show intolerance.

questions.s: Judging a whole group by the faults of a few of its members is called
o: reasoning
stereotyping
statistics
diplomacy
questions.e: Stereotyping assigns traits to everyone in a group. It ignores the individual and leads to unfair treatment.

questions.s: Treating a person unfairly because of his religion, gender or ethnic group is called
o: diversity
discrimination
moderation
regulation
questions.e: Discrimination is unequal treatment based on group identity. Prejudice is the attitude behind it.

questions.s: Which of these is the best response to hearing a hurtful joke about a minority group?
o: Make clear that it is not acceptable
Laugh along to avoid any awkwardness
Share the joke with other friends
Say nothing and quietly leave the room
questions.e: Speaking up discourages disrespect. Silence or laughter can signal approval.

questions.s: Rights and duties are related because
o: rights have no duties attached to them
every right carries a matching duty
duties exist only for people who are poor
rights are just the same as personal wishes
questions.e: If everyone has a right to safety, others have a duty not to harm. Rights work only when duties are respected.

questions.s: Which of these is a civic duty of a citizen?
o: Hiding income
Paying taxes honestly
Ignoring traffic laws
Damaging public parks
questions.e: Taxes finance public services that everyone uses. The others harm the community.

questions.s: Voting in an election is best described as
o: a duty of a responsible citizen
a complete waste of the citizen's valuable time
a favour that the citizen does to the candidates
an optional act that is meant only for the educated
questions.e: Taking part in choosing representatives is a way of sharing responsibility for the community. It is a right which citizens should use.

questions.s: Which of these shows good civic sense?
o: Spitting on the street near other people
Parking a car right across a neighbour's gate
Cutting into a queue ahead of those waiting
Throwing litter in a dustbin
questions.e: Using a bin keeps public spaces clean for all. The others inconvenience others.

questions.s: Waiting for your turn in a queue shows
o: weakness
poor planning
respect and fairness
lack of skill
questions.e: Each person's time matters equally. Cutting in takes an unfair advantage over others.

questions.s: A person who volunteers to clean a neighbourhood after a flood is showing
o: selfishness
a lack of ambition
dishonesty
service to the community
questions.e: Voluntary service helps others without payment. It strengthens trust among neighbours.

questions.s: Which is an example of an ethical use of social media?
o: Posting a private photo of a friend without permission
Sending anonymous threats
Spreading rumours as jokes
Verifying news before sharing
questions.e: Responsible use respects truth and privacy. Threats and rumours cause harm.

questions.s: A friend asks Zain to share the answers to an online test taken at home, saying that everyone does it. Zain should
o: share them, since everyone else is doing the same thing
share them, but only in return for some payment
decline, because honest results matter even if others cheat
agree to it, but tell no one else about the matter
questions.e: Wrong actions do not become right by being common. Honesty is judged by the act, not by how widespread it is.

questions.s: The argument 'everyone does it, so it is acceptable' is a poor moral argument because
o: the popularity of an act does not make it right
moral rules are changed by people every single day
only what the majority does can decide right and wrong
rules of conduct do not matter at all in daily life
questions.e: Popularity shows only what people do, not what they ought to do. Many accepted practices in history were later seen as unjust.

questions.s: Hoarding essential goods during a shortage to sell them later at a higher price is considered unethical because
o: it is simply a sign of good business sense
it shows thrift and careful planning for the future
it harms others who need the goods now
it follows the normal working of the law of demand
questions.e: Creating scarcity for profit denies others essentials and puts private gain above need.

questions.s: Which of the following describes environmental stewardship?
o: Using natural resources carefully so that future generations also benefit
Using as much of the available resources as possible while they last
Leaving the care of the environment entirely to chance and luck
Moving away to a fresh place whenever one place gets polluted
questions.e: Stewardship means caring for nature as a trust for the future. It rests on responsibility to those who will come after us.

questions.s: The idea that present generations should not use up resources in ways that harm future generations is called
o: intergenerational justice
retributive justice
procedural justice
market competition
questions.e: Intergenerational justice extends fairness across time. The other terms concern punishment, process or business.

questions.s: A factory owner could save money by avoiding costly filters, though smoke will harm nearby people. Which principle should guide his choice?
o: Maximise profit
Do no harm to others
Imitate competitors
Follow the cheapest option
questions.e: The duty not to harm others limits how far profit may be pursued. Doing what rivals do does not remove that duty.

questions.s: Cruelty to animals is considered
o: a matter of fashion and personal taste only
unethical in the major religious and moral traditions
allowed whenever it is done for the sake of entertainment
a sign of strength and courage in a person
questions.e: Compassion for living creatures is widely taught. It is therefore wrong to cause them needless suffering.

questions.s: Employing a child to work long hours in a factory instead of sending him to school is unethical because
o: children generally do not like going to school every day
it helps to improve the total output of the factory
it denies the child's right to education and safety
families in every case want it to be done this way
questions.e: Children have rights to protection and learning. Short-term income does not justify losing their future.

questions.s: Paying a worker a wage that is far below what was agreed is
o: a normal secret of business
a breach of fairness and trust
a sign of good economy
the worker's own fault for accepting
questions.e: Honouring agreements on pay is basic justice. Workers have a right to the wage they have earned.

questions.s: Which of the following is an example of fair dealing in trade?
o: Mixing cheaper material and selling as best
Using correct weights and measures
Hiding the price from the buyer
Changing labels on expired goods
questions.e: Honest weights give the buyer exactly what he pays for. The others deceive.

questions.s: Which of these is the main reason honesty matters in society?
o: It builds trust between people
It always brings a profit to the person who is honest
It is easy to practise in every situation
It avoids all difficulties for the person who practises it
questions.e: Trust makes cooperation possible in trade, law and family. Honesty may sometimes bring a loss, but it keeps trust.

questions.s: A person who tells a lie to avoid a small embarrassment has chosen
o: convenience over honesty
bravery
politeness
loyalty
questions.e: Honesty may feel uncomfortable, but a lie to escape embarrassment weakens trust. Politeness can be kept without untruth.

questions.s: Which of these best describes 'moderation' as an ethical virtue?
o: Never spending any money on oneself at any time
Eating only one meal in a whole day as a rule
Avoiding extremes in spending, eating and behaviour
Avoiding every kind of pleasure and comfort in life
questions.e: Moderation is balance, and is taught in many traditions. Extremes such as total denial are not what it means.

questions.s: Patience in ethical life means
o: giving up quickly whenever a task becomes hard
avoiding every kind of effort and exertion
showing anger whenever things do not go well
staying calm and persevering in difficulty
questions.e: Patience is the ability to endure difficulty without losing self-control. It supports good decisions.

questions.s: Which of the following shows respect for elders in a family?
o: Mocking their habits
Ignoring their advice automatically
Listening politely and helping them
Leaving them alone when ill
questions.e: Respect is shown by courtesy and care. Disrespect or neglect is wrong in every culture.

questions.s: Ayesha is fully qualified, and the post is advertised as open to all. A manager rejects her only because she is a woman. This is
o: fair selection
a business decision
good practice
gender discrimination
questions.e: Rejecting a qualified candidate because of her sex is unfair treatment on irrelevant grounds. Selection should be by merit.

questions.s: A person with a disability applies for a job he can do well. Ethical employers should
o: reject him in order to avoid any trouble
offer him less pay than the other workers
choose whichever candidate is the easiest
judge him on his ability to do the work
questions.e: Equal opportunity requires judging people on relevant skills, with fair adjustments where needed. Lower pay for the same work is unjust.

questions.s: Which of these is an example of a moral dilemma?
o: Choosing what to order for lunch from a long menu
Deciding between telling a painful truth and sparing a friend's feelings
Selecting the colour of a new shirt to buy
Choosing which route to take on the way to work
questions.e: A dilemma arises when two moral values conflict, so that any choice gives up something that matters. The others are ordinary preferences.

questions.s: When two duties conflict, the best approach is to
o: choose whichever duty is easier to carry out in practice
weigh the values and choose the course that prevents greater harm
do neither of the two duties and avoid the whole matter
ask which of the two choices will be noticed more by others
questions.e: Ethical reasoning means weighing consequences and principles carefully. Avoiding the decision or choosing what is visible is not a principled approach.

questions.s: A student is asked to lie to protect a classmate who is bullying others. Which duty should generally take priority?
o: The duty to prevent harm to the victims
The duty to keep a friend's secret at any cost
The duty to avoid conflict with other students
The duty to stay popular among all classmates
questions.e: Protecting people from harm outweighs keeping a secret that enables abuse. Loyalty does not justify supporting cruelty.

questions.s: Under the 'veil of ignorance', which rule would people most likely choose for hiring?
o: One that favours the powerful members of society
One based on merit and fairness for all
One that favours the wealthy members of society
One based on family ties and personal favours
questions.e: If you did not know your own position in society, you would want fair rules that protect you in any role. Rules favouring the powerful could harm you.

questions.s: Which approach reflects good moral reasoning on a contested public question?
o: Refusing to listen to anyone who disagrees with you
Following whichever voice happens to be the loudest
Examining arguments on both sides before judging
Deciding the matter according to the strength of one's anger
questions.e: Good reasoning relies on evidence and fair consideration of other views. It resists emotion or pressure.

questions.s: Which of the following is a sign of a person with good character?
o: He seeks fame at any cost
He keeps his word and treats people fairly
He changes his story to suit his listeners
He avoids responsibility
questions.e: Good character shows in reliable, fair conduct. Self-promotion or evasion shows weakness of character.

questions.s: If a gift to a poor family is given with humiliation, such as announcing it to the whole village, the ethical flaw is
o: the amount of the gift is too small for the family
it violates the receiver's dignity
it is given too early in the season of the year
it cannot be claimed against tax by the giver
questions.e: Help should respect the dignity of the receiver. Public humiliation turns charity into a display of power.

questions.s: Which of these is an essential element of a fair trial?
o: The verdict is decided before hearing
Only the accuser speaks
The judge is a relative of the accuser
The accused can present a defence
questions.e: A hearing of both sides is basic to fairness. An interested judge is a conflict of interest.

questions.s: The principle that no one should be a judge in his own case aims to
o: save time
prevent bias
reduce costs
protect experts
questions.e: If a judge has a stake, his decision may be biased. An impartial person is needed.

questions.s: Which of these best describes 'procedural fairness'?
o: Following fair steps that give everyone a hearing
Reaching the outcome that the powerful people want
Skipping the inquiry altogether in order to save time
Giving exactly the same result to everyone concerned
questions.e: Fair process matters even where outcomes differ. Identical results for all are not required.

questions.s: A company policy states that promotions depend on yearly assessment, but a manager promotes his friend without assessment. This is a failure of
o: equality of outcome
job rotation
salary scale
procedural fairness
questions.e: The rule was set, but not followed for one person. Applying procedures consistently is part of fairness.

questions.s: An honest citizen sees a neighbour dumping waste in a drain. A sensible first step is to
o: dump his own waste in the same drain as well
politely explain the harm and ask him to stop
shout abuse at the neighbour in front of others
ignore it for ever and say nothing at all
questions.e: A calm, respectful request often works and keeps good relations. If it continues, a complaint to the proper authority is appropriate.

questions.s: Moral responsibility requires that a person
o: acted under force that he was unable to resist
was entirely unaware of the situation around him
acted freely and knew what he was doing
was a very young child who could not understand
questions.e: Responsibility usually depends on freedom and knowledge. Force or lack of awareness reduces blame.

questions.s: A doctor refuses to prescribe an unnecessary expensive drug that would bring him a commission. His action shows
o: poor business sense in running a clinic
disloyalty to the company that makes the drug
putting the patient's interest first
lack of knowledge about the drugs on the market
questions.e: A professional should not let personal gain influence his advice. Putting the patient first is the core duty.

questions.s: Which of these is a violation of academic integrity?
o: Citing every source used in an essay
Asking the teacher for feedback on a first draft
Buying a ready-made project and submitting it
Studying with classmates in preparation for an exam
questions.e: Submitting purchased work claims credit for another's effort. The other actions are honest.

questions.s: What is the main purpose of ethical rules in a profession?
o: To limit the number of people who can join
To increase the fees that members may charge
To keep outsiders ignorant of the work done
To protect the public and maintain trust
questions.e: Professions earn trust by promising to behave fairly and competently. Without it, people could not safely rely on their services.

questions.s: A clerk is told that his promotion depends on silently approving a wrong payment. Which value is under test?
o: Generosity
Integrity
Curiosity
Punctuality
questions.e: Integrity means keeping to principle under pressure. The other values are not what is being tested.

questions.s: Which of these shows that a person has accepted responsibility for a mistake?
o: He blames the weather or bad luck for it
He waits patiently for others to forget it
He changes the subject whenever it is raised
He admits it and takes steps to correct it
questions.e: Admitting an error and acting to repair it is responsibility. Excuses or silence avoid it.

questions.s: Reputation is built mainly through
o: consistent honest conduct over time
advertising and public relations alone
the possession of great wealth
one single act of charity
questions.e: People judge character by long patterns of behaviour. Advertising can create an image but not a reputation that lasts.

questions.s: Which of these is an example of respectful disagreement?
o: Insulting the speaker in front of other people
Walking out of the room without saying a word
Giving reasons and listening to the other side
Shouting until the other side finally gives up
questions.e: Respectful disagreement addresses ideas and not persons. It allows learning even when views stay different.

questions.s: Which of the following would be a fair way to settle a dispute over a shared water channel between two villages?
o: Let the stronger village take all of the water
Negotiate a schedule agreed by both sides
Block the channel in secret during the night
Wait for the other village to give in on its own
questions.e: Negotiated sharing respects the needs of both. Force or secrecy creates lasting conflict.

questions.s: Which of these is a sign of intellectual honesty?
o: Admitting that one does not know
Pretending to know the answer to everything
Avoiding any questions that are difficult
Quoting only those facts that support one's view
questions.e: Intellectual honesty includes admitting limits and following evidence. Selective quoting misleads.

questions.s: A study finds that offering a bribe increases the chances of getting a licence. Why is it still unethical to bribe?
o: It costs too much money for the applicant in the long run
It is a slower route than the normal procedure
It undermines fairness and harms honest applicants
It is soon forgotten by everyone concerned in the matter
questions.e: Even if effective, bribery gives an unfair advantage and weakens public trust. Success does not make it right.

questions.s: Which of these examples shows 'public interest' guiding a private citizen?
o: Keeping quiet about the leak he has noticed
Reporting a gas leak in a crowded market
Closing his own shop and going home
Moving away from the area for a while
questions.e: Reporting a hazard protects many people. Staying silent leaves the risk in place.

questions.s: Which sentence expresses a principle shared by many religions and philosophies?
o: Success is the only true measure of a person's worth
Do not harm others and help those in need
Rules are meant only for the weak and the timid
Power alone decides what is right and what is wrong
questions.e: Avoiding harm and helping others appears across traditions and is widely accepted as a basis for morality.

questions.s: Which of these is a virtue?
o: Cruelty
Cheating
Greed
Courage
questions.e: Courage is a recognised virtue in many traditions. The others are vices.

questions.s: Which of these is a vice?
o: Kindness
Dishonesty
Fairness
Patience
questions.e: Dishonesty is a fault of character. The others are virtues.

questions.s: Which of the following is an example of kindness?
o: Ignoring a person who is in need of help
Making fun of a weaker person in the class
Helping an elderly person cross a busy road
Taking the front seat of a bus from a child
questions.e: Kindness is a caring act towards others. The others show unkindness.

questions.s: Which of the following shows respect for teachers?
o: Interrupting the lesson again and again
Mocking the teacher's dress behind his back
Skipping class every day for no reason
Listening attentively in class
questions.e: Attentive listening shows regard for the teacher and for learning. The other behaviours show disrespect.

questions.s: Sharing food with a hungry neighbour is an act of
o: ambition
rivalry
pride
generosity
questions.e: Generosity is giving without expecting something in return. It builds bonds in a community.

questions.s: What should a person do if he damages someone's property by accident?
o: Admit it and offer to pay for the repair
Run away before anyone can see
Blame some child who was standing nearby
Pretend that nothing has happened
questions.e: Taking responsibility for an accident is honest and fair. Running away adds dishonesty.

questions.s: Which of these religions originated in the Indian subcontinent?
o: Jainism
Judaism
Zoroastrianism
Christianity
questions.e: Jainism began in ancient India, as did Hinduism, Buddhism and Sikhism. Judaism arose in the Middle East, Zoroastrianism in ancient Persia and Christianity in Palestine.

questions.s: Which of these correctly matches a place of worship with its faith?
o: Gurdwara and Sikhism
Synagogue and Hinduism
Mandir and Judaism
Church and Buddhism
questions.e: A gurdwara is the Sikh house of worship. A synagogue is Jewish, a mandir is Hindu and a church is Christian.

questions.s: Which of these correctly matches a sacred text with its tradition?
o: Vedas and Judaism
Tripitaka and Buddhism
Avesta and Sikhism
Guru Granth Sahib and Hinduism
questions.e: The Tripitaka is the Buddhist canon. The Vedas are Hindu scriptures, the Avesta is Zoroastrian and the Guru Granth Sahib is the Sikh scripture.

questions.s: When teaching about another religion, the most respectful and accurate approach is to
o: rely on rumours about what its followers do in private
compare it unfavourably with one's own faith at every point
describe it as its followers do, using reliable sources
leave out the parts that one happens to dislike
questions.e: Fair description depends on reliable sources and on listening to believers themselves. Ranking faiths or relying on rumour distorts understanding.

questions.s: Under the Constitution of Pakistan, a citizen has the right to
o: follow any religion he likes without limit of any kind
follow only the religion that the state itself follows
profess and practise his religion, within law, order and morality
practise his faith in private only and never in public
questions.e: The Constitution guarantees freedom to profess and practise one's religion, subject to law, public order and morality. It does not restrict citizens to a single faith.

questions.s: Kant held that lying is wrong even when it might bring a good result. This view is best described as
o: utilitarian, since it counts only the results of acts
relativist, since it depends on the culture of the person
egoist, since it serves only the interest of the person
deontological, since it rests on duty, not outcome
questions.e: Deontology judges acts by whether they follow moral duty, and Kant held that truthfulness is a universal duty. A utilitarian might allow a lie for a good result.

questions.s: A virtue ethicist faced with a decision would most likely ask
o: Which choice would bring me the most money?
Which law would be the easiest one to follow?
What does the majority of people want here?
What would a person of good character do?
questions.e: Virtue ethics centres on character traits such as honesty and courage. Money, convenience and majority opinion are not its main concern.

questions.s: A candidate submits a certificate that he knows is false in order to get a job. This is
o: fraud that harms honest applicants
a clever strategy that shows initiative
acceptable if he is able to do the job well
a small error that does little harm to anyone
questions.e: False documents deceive the employer and take opportunities from honest candidates. Ability does not excuse dishonesty.

questions.s: Being answerable for one's actions and their results is called
o: popularity
creativity
negotiation
accountability
questions.e: Accountability means accepting responsibility and being able to explain one's conduct. Creativity is the ability to produce new ideas.

questions.s: Keeping private information that a client or patient has entrusted to you secure is called
o: publicity
transparency
confidentiality
negotiation
questions.e: Confidentiality is a core professional duty of doctors, lawyers and counsellors. It may be broken only in narrow cases where the law or serious danger requires.

questions.s: The 'rule of law' means that
o: rulers and senior officials may make exceptions for themselves
everyone, including officials, is bound by the same laws
only the poorer citizens are required to obey the laws
laws apply only to the people who live in large cities
questions.e: The rule of law protects against arbitrary power by making everyone equally subject to law. Exempting rulers or classes defeats the principle.

questions.s: Virtue ethics, developed by Aristotle, focuses mainly on
o: the character of the person acting
the results of the action that is carried out
the law that applies to the action in question
the opinion held by the majority of the people
questions.e: Virtue ethics asks what kind of person to be, stressing traits such as courage and justice. Judging by results belongs to consequentialism.

questions.s: In Hindu and Buddhist teaching, 'karma' means that
o: actions have moral consequences
fate cannot change
rituals matter more than conduct
knowledge is not important
questions.e: Karma teaches that deeds shape the future. It is not a belief in fixed fate.

questions.s: In Judaism, 'tzedakah' means
o: a festival held at the time of harvest
a ritual of cleansing before worship
a sacred scroll kept in a place of worship
charity and acts of justice
questions.e: Tzedakah comes from a root meaning righteousness. It is the duty to give to the poor.

questions.s: A shopkeeper gives Bilal Rs 500 extra change by mistake. What is the right thing to do?
o: Keep it, because the shopkeeper was careless and must bear the loss
Return it only if someone happens to be watching him
Point out the error and return the extra money
Keep it, but give a small part of it to charity
questions.e: The money does not belong to Bilal, so returning it is honest. A gift to charity from money that is not his own does not correct the mistake.

questions.s: A government clerk is offered a gift by a citizen whose application is pending. The best response is to
o: accept it and then process the file as quickly as he can
accept it, but take no action at all on the file
ask for a larger gift before he takes any action
decline it, since it may influence his decision
questions.e: A gift from someone who needs a decision can amount to a bribe or create a conflict of interest. Declining protects fairness and trust.

questions.s: Which of these is an example of respecting another person's privacy?
o: Sharing a colleague's home address with strangers on request
Taking a photo of someone and posting it without asking him
Not reading a friend's private messages without permission
Asking a neighbour how much income he earns each month
questions.e: Privacy means control over personal information. Reading messages without permission, or sharing information or images, violates it.

questions.s: A company discovers that its product has a minor safety defect that might harm few customers. It would cost a lot to recall. Which approach best matches ethical practice?
o: Inform customers and fix or recall the product
Wait for customers to complain about the defect before acting
Quietly stop selling it but say nothing to the buyers
Blame the customers for misusing the product in some way
questions.e: Customers have a right to know about risks. Silent withdrawal leaves existing buyers exposed.

questions.s: An employee is asked by his company to advertise a medicine with exaggerated claims. The ethical response is to
o: refuse to make false claims and propose accurate wording
do it, because the company is paying him for the work
do it, but put the claims in very small print
ask for more pay in exchange for making the false claims
questions.e: Advertising must not mislead, particularly about health. Smaller print still deceives.

questions.s: A new student, Daniel, from a Christian family joins a class of mostly Muslim students. Which behaviour best reflects respect for him?
o: Treat him as an equal member of the class
Ask him to sit apart from the other pupils
Question him again and again about his faith
Avoid talking to him in the corridor and class
questions.e: Equal respect means inclusion without prying or isolating. Citizens of all faiths share the same dignity.

questions.s: Mehwish discovers that she can see another person's email left open on a shared computer. The ethical action is to
o: read it out of mere curiosity while alone
log out without reading it
copy the contact list of the owner to a phone
send a message from it to a friend as a joke
questions.e: Respecting privacy means not looking at someone's private communications. Logging out also protects the owner.

questions.s: Which statement about workplace harassment is accurate?
o: It is wrong, and employers must provide a safe way to complain
It is a purely private matter between two individuals
It is acceptable if it is only meant as a joke
It affects only the senior staff members of an office
questions.e: Harassment violates dignity and safety. A workplace should have clear procedures to deal with complaints.

questions.s: Which of these best describes gender equality?
o: Men having all of the opportunities that life offers
Women having no responsibilities at all in society
Women and men having equal dignity and opportunity
Both sexes doing exactly the same kind of work always
questions.e: Equality means equal worth and fair opportunity, not identical roles. A society that denies girls education loses talent and fails justice.

questions.s: A person who gives a donation mainly so that others will praise him shows
o: perfect generosity of the very highest kind
a mixed motive that reduces the moral worth
honesty in the manner of giving the gift
humility before the person who receives it
questions.e: When a gift is made for show, the motive is self-regard. The act may help others but expresses less goodness than giving quietly.

questions.s: Which of the following is an example of a professional code of conduct?
o: Rules that doctors follow about patient care
A weekly list of things to buy at the grocery shop
A detailed plan for a holiday with the whole family
A family recipe handed down through the generations
questions.e: A code of conduct sets standards for professional behaviour. The other items are personal documents.

questions.s: A boy is asked by his elders to marry someone he has not met and feels unable to refuse. Which principle is relevant to his case?
o: Elders' wishes must always be final in this matter
Money and family wealth should decide the question
Tradition cannot be questioned in any way at all
Consent should be free and informed
questions.e: Marriage, in the law and ethics of most traditions, needs the free consent of those who marry. Respect for elders does not remove it.

questions.s: A person who always keeps his promises is considered
o: reliable
careless
dishonest
forgetful
questions.e: Keeping promises builds trust. Reliability is the quality of being dependable.

questions.s: A town can fund either a small hospital serving thousands or a large monument admired by a few. A utilitarian would favour the
o: monument, since it is more impressive to see
hospital, as it benefits the greatest number
monument, since it costs more to build
choice made by the oldest citizen of the town
questions.e: Utilitarianism compares the benefit and harm to everyone affected. The hospital does more good for more people.
